text: Existential means relating to existence itself — an existential crisis is one so serious it threatens whether something keeps existing at all. Losing the film wouldn't just have embarrassed Pixar: the studio didn't have the resources to survive a year's delay, so the deleted movie put the whole company's life on the line.
Cantankerous means bad-tempered, argumentative, and quick to complain — generally difficult to get along with. It's the article's affectionate jab at Mr. Potato Head, the grumpiest toy in the box.

To avert a disaster is to prevent it — to turn it away before it can do harm, like slamming the brakes to avert a crash. That's what Pixar's leaders huddled in a conference room to do: stop the loss of the movie from becoming permanent.

A “cast of characters” is normally the full list of roles in a movie or play. The joke here is that the movie about Woody and Buzz was saved by a real-life cast of characters — including, improbably, a 6-month-old baby.

To be chauffeured is to be driven somewhere by a personal driver, like a celebrity in a limo. The absurd image is the point: a computer, buckled into the back seat of a Volvo, being chauffeured across town like a VIP — because it held the last copy of the movie.

Intellectual property (IP) is a creation of the mind — a story, character, song, or invention — that the law treats as something a person or company owns. The computer itself was worth maybe a few thousand dollars; Woody, Buzz, and Mr. Potato Head, the characters stored inside it, were worth billions. That's why you can't legally make and sell your own Buzz Lightyear movie.
An installment is one part of a series delivered piece by piece — one episode, one sequel, one payment at a time. “Toy Story 5” is the latest installment of the franchise.

Iconic means so famous and widely recognized that it stands as a symbol of its whole category — an icon. “Toy Story” is iconic the way the Nike swoosh or the Star Wars theme is: everyone knows it on sight.

In entertainment, a franchise is a series of movies (plus the games, toys, and spinoffs) built around the same characters and world — Toy Story, Marvel, Pokémon. Different sense from a fast-food franchise, where someone pays for the right to run a local branch of a chain — though both come from the idea of a valuable name being extended outward.
Spud is slang for a potato. So “a cantankerous spud” is the article's playful way of saying Mr. Potato Head — a grumpy potato going up against a tablet.

In computing, a “string” is a sequence of typed characters — letters, symbols, numbers in a row. The string here, /bin/rm -r -f *, is a real Unix command, and the article translates it exactly: delete everything, everywhere, by force, without asking. One line, one wrong place, ninety percent of a movie gone.

A directory is what we now usually call a folder — a named container for files on a computer. The whole catastrophe came down to directories: the delete command was meant for someone's personal directory but ran in the master one holding the movie.

Nuked is slang for destroyed completely and instantly — from “nuclear.” The command nuked “Toy Story 2” in about the length of one song: years of work erased in the time it takes to play “You've Got a Friend in Me.”

Cloud computing means storing files and running programs on distant internet servers instead of your own machine — the reason your photos survive even if your phone dies. In 1998 none of that existed: Pixar's movie lived on a handful of physical computers in one building, which is why one command could destroy it.

A “master” copy is the original, official version that everything else is copied from — the master drive held the one true “Toy Story 2.” That's what made the deletion so devastating: this wasn't somebody's personal copy, it was the source.

To be cranking away at something is to be working on it hard and steadily, like turning a crank over and over. Oren Jacob was cranking away on the movie when the files started vanishing before his eyes.

To vaporize is to turn into vapor — to disappear into thin air, instantly and completely. “You don't often watch a company vaporize in front of your eyes” is Jacob's way of saying he wasn't just watching files disappear; he was watching Pixar's future evaporate with them.

Hysteria is wild, uncontrolled panic — emotion so strong it drowns out thinking. Susman's line is the article's calm center: “hysteria is never going to be a productive way of dealing with things.” While Jacob lost his mind, she started asking questions.
Kaput (borrowed from German) means broken, ruined, finished — done for. A movie going kaput would sting at any studio; at Pixar in 1999, it threatened the company's existence.

A direct-to-video movie skips theaters entirely and goes straight to home video — historically the budget path for sequels nobody expected much from. Pixar had fought to give “Toy Story 2” a real theatrical release instead, which raised the stakes: a hard deadline, and no quiet way to fail.

Counterintuitive means the opposite of what your gut expects — it runs counter to intuition. Releasing a sequel in theaters instead of direct-to-video felt like a strange bet at the time; it turned out to be one of the best calls Pixar ever made.

To stare down a threat is to face it directly, eye to eye, like a gunslinger in a western. Pixar was staring down the possibility of blowing its deadline and delaying the sequel a full year — which its co-founder says would have been catastrophic.

To blow a deadline is to miss it — “blow” as in blowing a chance or blowing a lead. For most projects that means an awkward apology; for Pixar it meant a year's delay the company couldn't afford to survive.

Here absorb means to take a hit and keep functioning — the way a boxer absorbs a punch or a sponge absorbs a spill. Catmull's point is brutal accounting: Pixar simply didn't have the money to absorb a year-long delay and survive it.

To salvage is to rescue what can still be saved from a wreck — the word originally described recovering cargo from sunken ships. With the blame question deliberately set aside, all that mattered was salvaging the film.

“As it happens” flags a lucky coincidence — by chance, it turned out that way. As it happens, Susman had a new baby at home, which is the only reason a full copy of the movie existed outside Pixar's walls.

Parental leave is time off from work to care for a new baby. Susman's work-from-home setup — built so she could keep working after her son's bedtime once her leave ended — accidentally became the backup system that saved the film.

To lug something is to haul it with effort — it's heavy, awkward, and you feel every step. Once a week Susman lugged the hulking computer into the office to download the latest version of the film. That weekly chore turned out to be worth billions.
Hulking means massive and bulky — built like the Hulk. Computers in 1998 weren't sleek laptops; hers was a hulking machine you needed real muscle to move.

To smother is to cover something completely — usually it means dangerously (smothering a fire, or a person), but here it's protective: they smothered the computer in pillows and blankets like a newborn, because one pothole could have killed the last copy of the movie.

Hazard lights are a car's both-blinkers-at-once flashers, used to warn other drivers you're moving slowly or stopped. Denied a police escort, they drove the precious cargo home-brewed style: slowly, hazards flashing, the computer belted in like a passenger.

To flicker to life is to start up hesitantly — screen blinking, not quite steady — the way an old machine wakes. After the drive across town, the computer flickered to life and brought Woody and Buzz back from the dead.
A wink at Buzz Lightyear's catchphrase, “To infinity and beyond!” The article says the sigh of relief could be heard “from infinity and beyond” — a Toy Story–sized exhale.

Raves here are wildly enthusiastic reviews — critics “raving” means gushing with praise, not going to a dance party. “Opened to universal raves” means essentially every reviewer loved it, less than a year after the movie had been deleted twice.

To overhaul something is to take it apart and rebuild it thoroughly — not a touch-up, a teardown. After saving the deleted film, Pixar's executives deleted it again on purpose and overhauled the story itself — what Catmull called “the cinematic equivalent of a heart transplant.”

To pull something off is to succeed at something so difficult it seemed impossible. Rebuilding a whole movie in under a year, right after nearly losing it forever — they pulled it off, and Susman still thinks it's the best film of the franchise.

Families of powerful operating systems favored by engineers and studios — the systems behind most of the world's servers (Linux is the free descendant of Unix's design). Their command line is famously powerful and famously unforgiving: commands like rm delete instantly, no Recycle Bin, no undo.

A station wagon is a long family car with a big cargo area behind the back seats — the minivan's ancestor. History's least glamorous rescue vehicle: a Volvo wagon carrying the only copy of a billion-dollar movie.
The co-founder of Apple — and, at the time, Pixar's chairman and owner. During the rescue weekend, one of the most famous executives in tech history was the guy pouring the coffee.
